source: Lamar's Counter Cheat Sheets - Spotting Fakes (Business Plan and Operations). That document is the full version; these are its 60-second checks. Both are generated from sheets-source.json.
law: Selling or offering goods under a counterfeit trademark, knowing it, is a crime in Florida (§831.032). It is a felony at 100 items or $2,500 of retail value.

sheets.title: Ground rules for anything with a big name on it
sheets.why: Brand names are what fakers copy, and a fake costs whatever was paid for it. These rules apply to every sheet that follows.
checks: The name is not the collateral until it is proven. Price what you can verify today: the metal, the weight, a cert that matches. Everything else is a no-name item.
Ask where it came from and how long he has had it. A real owner answers easily. Write the answer on the ticket.
Check the price against the market. "New" at half price is the most common tell on every sheet.
Run the sheet for that item. Use the free lookup it lists, and type the number in yourself.

sheets.title: Gold and silver jewelry
sheets.why: Fakes are plated base metal, sometimes tungsten, stamped 14K, 18K or 925. We pay by metal weight, so a fake costs everything paid.
checks: Weigh it in grams.
Loupe the stamp for a karat or 925 mark plus a maker's mark. US law requires both, so a missing one is a warning sign.
Magnet: if the piece is pulled (not just the clasp spring), no gold price.
File a notch and put acid in the notch. Plating passes a surface test.

lookup.where: No serial lookup exists, and Tiffany doesn't authenticate. Compare the design on jamesavery.com ("Designs From Our Archives"), tiffany.com, pandora.net or davidyurman.com.

sheets.rule: pay nothing extra for a brand name, and no notch allowed means no deal.

sheets.title: Gold and silver coins and bars (bullion)
sheets.why: Chinese fakers copy Eagles, Morgans and bars, and even the grading holders. We pay close to melt, so one fake costs nearly everything paid.
checks: Weigh it in grams and check the table. Fakes are often a little off. A 1 oz Gold Eagle or Krugerrand weighs about 33.93 g, not 31.1 g, because it is 22K alloy.
Calipers: diameter against the table, thickness against a coin you know is real.
Magnet: nothing should stick. On silver, do the slide test: tilt the piece about 45 degrees and set the magnet on it. On real silver it slides down slowly instead of sticking.

Sigma verifier, if the store buys one (coins and bars only, from $999): set the metal and size, then test both sides. It reads through flips, slabs and assay cards. Without one, lean harder on weight, calipers and the slab lookup.
Loupe the date and mint mark (the small letter for the mint that made it). Check that the pair exists (see "Dates that exist").

lookup.where: ngccoin.com/certlookup. Enter the cert number and grade. Most coins graded since 2008 have photos.
pcgs.com/cert, or the free PCGS app (barcode scan or NFC tap). NGC also has a free app.
scan a Veriscan-marked PAMP bar.
check that a date and mint mark exist.

sheets.rule: buy gold bars over 1 oz only after an outside test. Even a Sigma can't see a deep tungsten core.

sheets.title: Diamonds and gemstones
sheets.why: A claimed diamond may be moissanite (a lab-made look-alike), cubic zirconia (CZ), glass, white sapphire or lab-grown (real diamond, factory-made); Lamar's does not pay for stones, but know what you hold.
checks: Say the rule first: we pay on the metal; the stone rides free.

Multi-tester (reads heat and electrical flow). Stone clean, dry, room temperature. Fingers on the tester's metal grips. Tip square to the table (big top facet), firm pressure. Loose stone: set it on the metal rest and hold the rest.
Diamond: natural or lab-grown. It cannot tell them apart.
Moissanite: moissanite, the tip touched metal, or rarely a lab-grown diamond. Retest.
Neither: CZ, glass, white sapphire or similar.
Loupe the band. "CZ" stamped means cubic zirconia. A stone set in silver (925, STER) is usually an imitation. Metal is a clue, not proof.

sheets.title: Rolex and luxury watches
sheets.why: Fake Rolexes are common, the best ("superclones") pass most counter checks, and one bad loan costs thousands.
checks: Seconds hand. A modern Rolex sweeps in small, fast steps. One tick a second means quartz: fake, unless a real Oysterquartz.
Back. Most models: solid and plain. A clear back is rare (the 1908 has one).
Cyclops (magnifying bubble over the date): date fills it, dead center. Small or off-center date means fake.
Loupe the dial. Printing crisp and slightly raised, markers straight. Fuzzy or crooked: fake.

sheets.title: Sports cards and Pokémon cards
sheets.why: Graded cases, vintage stars, modern autograph cards and Pokémon cards are all faked, and even a real card's price depends on its condition.
checks: Slab (sealed grading case): enter the cert number in the grader's free lookup. Card, year and grade must match the label.
The lookup photo must match the card in hand: centering, print specks, corner nicks. Fakers reuse real cert numbers. Older certs may lack photos.
Squeeze the case. Real ones are stiff; flex, cloudy seams, cracks or glue mean it was opened.
Raw (ungraded) vintage card: under the loupe, real post-war cards show a crisp rosette (a honeycomb of color dots). Blurry, muddy or pixel-like dots mean a copy.

sheets.rule: lend only on cards graded by PSA, BGS, SGC or CGC whose cert and photo match the card.

sheets.title: Autographs and memorabilia
sheets.why: Signed balls, photos, jerseys and "game-used" gear are forged in bulk, often with printed certificates to match, and a fake signature leaves an item worth only what it would be unsigned.
checks: Find the authenticator's sticker or hologram and its matching card or letter. Only five count: PSA/DNA, JSA, Beckett (BAS), MLB Authentication and Fanatics.
Look up the number free (below). The signer and the kind of item (ball, bat, photo, jersey) must match. A real number from another item means a fake.
A sticker that looks peeled, cut, lifted or reprinted fails. Real PSA/DNA stickers break apart if moved (older ones show a checkerboard). MLB holograms show tampering if removed.
None of the five? Value it as unsigned.

sheets.rule: value anything without a real third-party cert (one of the five, matching on lookup) as if unsigned.

sheets.title: Red dots, holographic sights and scopes
sheets.why: Airsoft copies of EOTech, Aimpoint, Trijicon and big-name scopes look right on a rifle, and a loan on one is a total loss.
checks: Dot color. Aimpoint: red only. EOTech: red or green, never switchable. A red/green switch means fake.
Front glass. EOTech: flat and dark; fakes are curved and mirror the room lights. Aimpoint: looks red (maybe orange or green), never blue or clear. A visible LED inside means fake.
Serial. Aimpoint: engraved on the side, same as the box. EOTech: sticker on the bottom. Missing or crude means fake.
Battery. EOTech takes only CR123, AA or N cell. Hearing-aid button cells, or a solar panel on an "Aimpoint," mean fake.

sheets.title: Power tool batteries and tools
sheets.why: Counterfeit Milwaukee M18, DeWalt 20V, Makita 18V and Ryobi ONE+ packs sell cheap online, hold far less than the label says, and can catch fire.
checks: Labels. Blurry, off-center, peeling or misspelled print, or commas in web addresses (DeWalt), mean fake.
Screws (DeWalt): genuine are silver and domed; fakes are flatter with a black coating.
Makita: black; logo and "Lithium-Ion" on both sides; logo and a white plug on the bottom; a red stripe inside the pressed latch.
Ryobi: the R and B in "RYOBI" have indents; model, serial and safety marks printed on it.
Fuel gauge (Milwaukee): genuine lights step up one by one; a fake lights all at once, dimmer.

lookup.where: warranty runs on the date code; no registration needed.

sheets.rule: a pack with fake tells gets $0 and goes back to the customer, never onto the shelf (the Power Tool Institute calls counterfeits illegal). Every other pack is priced on its load test.

sheets.title: Other things that get faked
sheets.why: YETI, Oakley, Ray-Ban, designer bags, Jordans and premium knives are copied well enough to pass a glance; these checks catch only lazy fakes.
checks: Price. "New" at a big discount is the top tell. Chris Reeve never discounts, Louis Vuitton rarely does, and Ray-Ban's owner sets minimum advertised prices.
Print and spelling. Logos crisp, words spelled right. A misspelling means fake.
Maker's marks where they belong (below). Missing is a warning sign.
